When AI is confidently wrong and what data teams can do about it
Tomas Hubka
Last updated: Oct 23, 2026
min read
Listen
10 s
10 s
1x
The real risk with AI-assisted analysis isn’t that the output is wrong. It’s that it’s wrong confidently. Here’s how to catch it before it ships into a decision.
Over the past couple of weeks, we've been working through three sides of the same question: how data work in game studios is changing as AI moves into the stack. I started with
the role shift itself
, looking at what parts of a data analyst’s job are being automated and what the role actually becomes next. Francesco covered the architectural side in
how to give an AI agent access to your game data
without creating risk. And I came back last week with
why dashboards aren’t enough anymore
and what AI agents unlock instead.
What’s missing from all three is the question that keeps surfacing when I talk to studios that are putting these tools into production: how much do you trust the output? That’s what this piece is about.
Felix Rieseberg, who leads engineering for Claude at Anthropic, addressed this quite clearly. The relevant section of his interview is embedded below, and the rest of this piece builds on it.
The problem isn’t that AI is wrong, it's the confidence
A junior analyst’s failure mode is obvious. They hedge, second-guess, and even add caveats. The uncertainty is visible, which gives the senior analyst a chance to probe. Current-generation AI tools produce fluent, well-formatted, authoritative-sounding output whether the answer is right or wrong, and by the time someone reads it, there’s no visible signal distinguishing high-confidence correct from high-confidence hallucination. So quite the opposite from the juniors.
Felix frames the risk this way in his interview:
If the model just guesses a temperature and is correct, that should not be a passing grade. That should be bad. We should rethink what we’re doing here. But if the model is actually off by half a degree but it really figured out the right location, figured out some reputable data sources and the way it got there was reputable and good, that should actually be better than a good result.
This isn’t a bug waiting for a patch. OpenAI’s own research paper
Why Language Models Hallucinate
makes the structural case: current training methods reward confident guessing over honest uncertainty (actively!). A model that says “I don’t know” gets scored lower than a model that produces a plausible-sounding wrong answer. The confidence isn’t a mistake, it’s a feature of how these systems are built. Stanford HAI’s
2026 AI Index
adds that AI agents fail roughly one in three structured attempts once conditions get more realistic than clean benchmark tasks, and it
compounds
when multiple agents interact: errors introduced by one get accepted as fact by the next.
Benn Stancil’s recent piece
Can analysis ever be automated?
names why this is especially hard in data work. Most software is self-validating: if the code runs, it runs. As Benn puts it, analysis is the opposite:
There’s no way to know if a chart ‘works’ unless you understand how it was built... we can only judge it by proxy: Do its conclusions sound plausible enough? Does it look like it was carefully made? Who made it?
That proxy test is exactly the test modern AI tools pass most easily. The craft markers that used to signal rigor now signal nothing, because they can be reproduced at zero cost whether the underlying analysis is correct or not. Alteryx’s
2026 State of the Data Analyst report
backs this up from the practitioner side: analysts aren’t being replaced, but a meaningful share of their week now goes to validating AI output rather than producing it.
How do you catch the confident mistakes?
Most of what works here isn’t new, but data teams can no longer afford being casual about it:
Start with the rule from the interview:
Felix: I rarely want the current session to judge itself. The current Claude session tends to be quite bad at being a judge of whether or not the work it did was quite good.
The thread that produced an answer will almost always defend it, and will do so convincingly.
